name: Sprint/HIIT for growth hormone

lead: Some teens do sprints or interval training because intense exercise raises growth hormone, which is involved in childhood growth.
The exercise-GH link is documented, but no published trial has tested whether such workouts change adult height.

paras: Vigorous exercise is a recognised stimulus of GH pulses, and GH acts on growth cartilage directly and through IGF-1. Believers extend this to a height effect; reference sources do not report that extension.

Sprint and interval training carry the usual risks of high-intensity exercise such as muscle and tendon strain. Adult height is described as largely genetic, with nutrition and health as the main modifiable factors.

lead: Sprint or high-intensity interval training (HIIT) for growth hormone is a height-related practice in looksmaxxing communities in which teenagers do all-out sprints or interval workouts in the belief that the resulting surge in growth hormone (GH) will help them grow taller. The idea rests on the fact that vigorous exercise is a recognised stimulus of GH secretion.[1]

Reference sources describe GH as the hormone most associated with childhood growth, acting on cartilage cells directly and through IGF-1 produced by the liver.[1] The same sources list vigorous exercise among the stimuli of GH release but do not state that exercise-triggered GH pulses change final adult height.[1] Adult height is described as largely genetic, with nutrition and health during childhood as the main environmental factors.[2]
No published trial was found that tests sprint or HIIT training as a way to increase final height in healthy adolescents.

paras: Practitioners describe short, maximal-effort sprints, hill sprints or interval circuits performed several times a week, sometimes combined with sleep and nutrition routines, with the stated aim of maximising natural GH release during the years when growth is still possible.

GH is released in pulses and is stimulated by sleep, nutrition, certain hormones and vigorous exercise.[1] In children, GH deficiency causes growth failure and short stature, which is the basis for the idea that more GH could mean more height.[1]

Twin studies cited in reference works estimate that 60 to 80 percent of height variation within a population is heritable, and growth in females is described as reaching zero on average around age 15 or 16 and in males around 18 to 19.[2] Chronic malnutrition during childhood is associated with reduced adult height.[2]

No studies found. Reference sources note that exercise raises GH levels temporarily, but no published trial has measured whether sprint or HIIT programmes alter final height in healthy adolescents.[1]

lore.intro: In height-focused forum discussion, sprinting and HIIT are often listed among free or natural ways to support growth during puberty.

claims.claim: Sprinting spikes GH, so it makes teens taller
